issues.text: The main results rest on a very small sample (roughly 50-60 annual observations) with many parameters (at least 7-8), so the asymptotic approximations justifying the frequentist confidence intervals may not hold and inference may be unreliable.
issues.quote: BK's main analysis is conducted with a small sample size (roughly 50-60 years) and their model contains many parameters (at least 8), which make careful inference and extensive robustness checks crucial.

issues.text: The evaluator asks for simulation evidence showing that the approach to quantifying statistical uncertainty yields valid confidence intervals in a setting with time series, few observations and many parameters; a heteroskedasticity-robust small-sample correction may also be needed.
issues.quote: I would suggest providing simulation evidence to illustrate the validity of their confidence regions in their setting, with time series data, few observations, and lots of parameters.

issues.text: The comparison with previous local-temperature estimates is artificial: the local model is linear and has no permanent growth effect, whereas the studies being compared to allow non-linear or permanent effects, so the comparison may be confounded.
issues.quote: they compare their results to those from a model that doesn't allow for non-linear effects or for permanent growth effects, which contrasts with the models used in those previous analyses. This may confound their comparison to previous work.

issues.text: The assumption that in-sample relationships between global temperature and extreme events remain valid under climate change is questionable; if the covariance changes, damage projections built on past covariances are invalid.
issues.quote: If climate change alters the relationship between global average temperature and extreme events, this assumption is invalid.

issues.text: Assuming temperature impacts vanish after 10 periods conflicts with the figures, which show GDP not fully reverted after 10 years (e.g. drought effects in Figure A.13, persistent impacts in SE Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa), and with prior studies assuming permanent growth effects; this may bias the SCC.
issues.quote: Qualitatively, GDP does not seem to have fully reverted to the mean after 10 years in BK's main figures.

issues.text: The extreme event thresholds (baseline probabilities of 0.05, 0.25, 0.01, 0.01) are not justified and the robustness of results to alternative thresholds is not shown.
issues.quote: Where do these come from? Are the results robust to other thresholds?

issues.text: The asymmetric hot/cold shock specification appears only as a robustness check (Figure A.9) and is not used in the main analysis; country-level and extreme-event impacts under this specification should be shown given evidence of non-linear temperature impacts.
issues.quote: However, this specification is not used apart from in this robustness check.

issues.text: The two-step procedure (AR-based residuals as temperature shocks) is confusing for readers from the climate impacts literature and is numerically equivalent to a one-step model with controls; the main model could be reformulated for clarity.
issues.quote: It could be easier to understand if the main model was swapped to this one, so it can be estimated in one step.

issues.text: Extrapolating in-sample relationships to future climates ignores possible tipping points and unmodelled adaptation or technology changes, which could push damages in either direction; the policy magnitude discussion needs these caveats, especially since identifying variation is small relative to projected climate change.
issues.quote: they are extrapolating the impacts of small deviations in weather to project the effect of large changes in climate.

issues.text: Using only GDP omits non-market damages, which other studies find to be the largest component of the social cost of carbon, so total damages may be substantially undercounted.
issues.quote: Therefore, using only GDP to estimate the impacts of climate change may severely undercount total damages needed for an SCC calculation.

issues.text: The evaluator questions how the paper reconciles its reported BHM impact figures (1-2% at 1C) with BHM's own projection of around 25% global GDP damage under RCP8.5, requesting clarification of the calculation.
issues.quote: It would be good to know how specifically how they calculate that BHM only find this smaller value

issues.text: It is unclear whether country-level panel regressions with non-linear effects and the extra extreme-event variables would produce SCC estimates as large as the global approach; the source of the large SCC difference needs clarifying.
issues.quote: Does running country level regressions (using panel regression models and non-linear effects) with the extra four extreme climate variables increase SCC estimates to a similar magnitude as when BK use global temperature directly?

issues.text: The paper does not analyse how extreme event frequencies are trending in the sample or projected to trend under climate models (e.g. CMIP), so the validity of projecting damages from historical covariances is unverified; the evaluator suggests citing or analysing projections.
issues.quote: It would be good to include some citations or analysis of CMIP projections to check how / if this could bias projected estimates.
